item.title: Systematic and dynamic task coding in the frontal cortex
item.description:
Relevance: 38% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Park, J., Park, H.-B., Holmes, C. D., Snyder, L. H.
Behavioral flexibility depends on the capacity to form and utilize task representations. Prior work has shown that baseline activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) can differ between two tasks. Comparing more than two tasks makes it possible to ask whether different neuronal populations share a common form of task encoding, that is, a conserved representational geometry across tasks. We trained two rhesus monkeys to perform 6 cognitive tasks and recorded spiking activity simultaneously from hundreds of neurons in the frontal eye field (FEF) or the dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC), one area per session. During the fixation period, before any task-specific stimulus appeared, the population activity state already reflected the upcoming task, and task identity could be decoded on single trials. Strikingly, the geometry of the 6 task states was conserved across populations recorded in different sessions, across the two areas, and across the two monkeys. Global signals that differ between tasks, such as expected reward, task difficulty, and attention, measured by reward amount, hit rate, and reaction time, did not fully account for this shared geometry. These findings suggest that the frontal cortex systematically adjusts its population state to encode and prepare for the upcoming task.

item.title: Prototypes of the Mind: A Unified Framework for Probing the Visual Brain
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Shi Chen, Seoyoung Ahn, Doris Tsao
arXiv:2611.15046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning has driven substantial progress in modeling fMRI responses, yet most existing approaches are optimized for a single objective---such as neural encoding, stimulus decoding, or post hoc interpretation---making it difficult to obtain a coherent account of neural representations. We introduce a unified framework that connects vision foundation models to brain activity while supporting neural analysis from multiple complementary perspectives. Our approach replaces black-box features with a sparse, interpretable representation composed of visual prototypes, and links these prototypes to voxel responses through a linear readout. This design makes the model transparent at both levels: prototype activations expose the visual concepts present in the stimulus, while the learned linear weights characterize each voxel's selectivity. Using this interface, we identify which visual concepts drive neural responses and where they appear in the image, reveal cortical organization through voxel tuning in prototype space, and perform controlled stimulus synthesis to probe cortical selectivity through targeted interventions. Together, these results establish prototype-based representations as a unified and interpretable foundation for studying visual representations in the human brain.

item.title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: arXiv AI
Qi Zhang, Bohan Wang, Qianru Sun, Hanwang Zhang
arXiv:2611.14942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.

item.title: A common neural axis links image distinctiveness and memorability
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Utochkin, I., Chang, W., Vogel, E. K., Awh, E.
Stimulus-specific memorability, the tendency for people to remember and forget the same stimuli, is a powerful predictor of memory performance that is independent of the study and retrieval factors that have dominated memory research. Critically, memorability can be defined in two ways: "Hit-ability" (H-ability) and "false alarm-ability" (FA-ability), the probability of correctly recognizing studied items or falsely recognizing unstudied items, respectively. Although past work has suggested that these are dissociable facets of memorability, challenging single-factor explanations, we present neural and computational evidence that they share a common neural axis. The neural signature of high H-ability matched the signature for low FA-ability, showing that these parameters have inverse relationships with a common factor. Moreover, we show that image distinctiveness predicts the flipped relationship between H-ability and FA-ability in both behavior and neural activity, providing a unifying explanation of stimulus-specific memorability.

item.title: Learned associations constrain anticipatory visual dynamics and enhance sensory and motor readiness to facilitate perceptual decisions
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Zhang, L., Yuan, M., Zhang, H., Morris Moscovitch, M., Alain, C.
Learned cue target associations can guide attention to facilitate perceptual decision making, yet how they shape the content and dynamics of neural activity, and whether this facilitation reflects anticipatory preparation, post-target sensory enhancement, or both, remains unclear. Here, we used magnetoencephalography while participants made living/nonliving judgments about visual objects (e.g., cat/violin) with left- or right-hand button presses. Cue category associations were established through repeated pairings: predictive cues always preceded one target category, whereas uninformative cues preceded both categories equally often. Predictive cues facilitated behavioral responses despite limited explicit awareness of the learned associations. Representational similarity analysis showed that prediction preactivated target-specific representations in the visual cortex resembling target evoked activity before target onset. Prediction also elicited anticipatory, response specific motor beta suppression. Together, these findings supported anticipatory preparation, with little evidence of enhanced posttarget visual specificity. Posttarget visual specificity and anticipatory motor preparation independently predicted response speed, with hierarchical drift diffusion modeling linking greater visual specificity to faster evidence accumulation and stronger motor preparation to shorter nondecision time (a model parameter reflecting sensory encoding and motor execution). Beyond representational content, prediction also constrained the evolution of anticipatory visual population activity, and more constrained, stable early visual trajectories predicted faster responses. These population dynamics were associated with faster evidence accumulation, lower decision thresholds, and shorter non-decision time. Together, these findings suggest that associative memory facilitates perceptual decisions by shaping the content and dynamics of anticipatory neural activity, with partially dissociable contributions from visual processing and motor preparation.

item.title: How striatal neurons influence decision-making depends on broader circuit context: evidence from theory-driven cell type identification
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Yu, Z., Verstynen, T., Rubin, J.
Neural cell types are often conceived as having fixed computational roles, yet their behavioral contributions may depend on the broader circuit state. In the striatum, for example, direct and indirect pathway spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are typically described as facilitating or suppressing actions, respectively. However, emerging observations of striatal activity, such as modulation related to action timing, action vigor, and reactive inhibition, call this dichotomy into question. Here we develop a state-space framework linking striatal population activity to decision dynamics by combining a spiking cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic (CBGT) model with large-scale in vivo recordings from mice performing a two-choice task. Modeled activity patterns guided the inference of putative striatal SPN subtypes in the empirical recordings, enabling reconstruction of decision trajectories through an underlying state space. Across simulated and experimental data, these trajectories revealed a shared set of decision dynamics and identified three state-dependent roles of indirect pathway activity: preserving uncertainty when active alone, signifying choice commitment when coactive with the direct pathway in the same action channel, and slowing decisions when recruited in the opposing channel. To interpret these roles mechanistically, we mapped state transitions onto previously described basal ganglia control ensembles (responsiveness, pliancy, and choice) that translate circuit activity into the evidence accumulation process, and we found that each role was associated with a distinct pattern of control ensemble engagement that tunes decision policy. These analyses support a context-dependent view of SPN function, in which their moment-to-moment impact emerges from the evolving profile of dynamics throughout the CBGT circuit.

item.title: Same Movements, Different Skills: How Context Shapes Learning in Humans and Neural Networks
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Gupta, M. W., Taylor, J. A.
What determines whether experiences are integrated into shared representations or split? Motor skill learning offers a revealing test: when two tasks require an identical sequence of movements, both intuition and theory suggest that practice in one should generalize to the other. Yet we find that changing context can make identical movements different skills. In simple recurrent networks trained on the same sequence across contexts, splitting was greatest when strong contextual inputs coincided with a high initial weight scale; neither alone sufficed. Greater representational separation coincided with separate context-specific learning curves. Humans practicing the same finger sequence while alternating between two performance-irrelevant contexts likewise exhibited context-specific curves, rather than the single continuous trajectory observed when practicing in a single context. State-space modeling favored split learning states in humans and very weakly coupled states in the most context-dependent networks. These findings have broader implications for understanding how learning generalizes across contexts.

item.title: What does it mean to understand language?
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Colton Casto, Anna Ivanova, Evelina Fedorenko, Nancy Kanwisher
arXiv:2511.19757v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language understanding entails not just extracting the surface-level meaning of the linguistic input, but constructing rich mental models of the situation it describes. Here we propose that because processing within the brain's core language system is fundamentally limited, deeply understanding language requires exporting information from the language system to other brain regions that construct mental models of minds, objects, and places, and that compute perceptual and motor representations. Building on earlier theorizing and empirical work, we argue that recent progress in cognitive neuroscience provides both the conceptual foundation and the methods to directly evaluate this hypothesis, thus opening up a new strategy to reveal what it means, cognitively and neurally, to understand language.

item.title: Lilith: Developmental Modular LLMs with Chemical Signaling
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv AI
Mohid Farooqi, Alejandro Comas-Leon
arXiv:2507.04575v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Current paradigms in Artificial Intelligence rely on layers of feedforward networks which model brain activity at the neuronal level. We conjecture that expanding to the level of multiple brain regions with chemical signaling may be a productive step toward understanding the emergence of consciousness. We propose LILITH, a novel architecture that combines developmental training of modular language models with brain-inspired token-based communication protocols, mirroring chemical signaling in the brain. Our approach models distinct brain regions as specialized LLM modules including thinking, memory, sensory, and regulatory components that communicate through emergent token-based signaling protocols analogous to neurotransmitter networks. Unlike traditional pre-trained systems, LILITH would employ developmental training where untrained LLM architectures learn through simulated life experiences, developing communication pathways and cognitive abilities through environmental interaction and evolutionary optimization. This framework would enable direct empirical investigation of consciousness emergence using Integrated Information Theory metrics while providing unprecedented insight into inter-module signaling patterns during development. By optimizing for consciousness emergence rather than task performance, LILITH could provide insight into different emergent phenomena at multiple levels of neural correlates, contrasting neuronal-level processing with multi-region coordination dynamics. The goal of this paper is to put the idea forward while recognizing the substantial challenges in implementing such a system.

item.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv AI
Fabrizia Giulia Garavaglia, Marco Giunti
arXiv:2611.16057v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

item.title: Linking Rapid Learning to Compositional Structure in Neural Networks: Evidence from Additive Analogies in Meta-Learned Parameter Spaces
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Abigail L. Tenenbaum, R. Thomas McCoy
arXiv:2611.17314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly. We study neural networks that have been optimized via meta-learning, a technique that exposes a network to many related functions to facilitate its subsequent learning of similar functions. Prior work has shown that these meta-learned networks can learn new functions rapidly, but how they do so remains unclear. To investigate their internal structure, we take inspiration from classic work demonstrating additive relationships among the learned vectors that neural networks use to represent words (e.g., "king" minus "man" plus "woman" approximates "queen"). Analogously, we look for additive relationships among a meta-learned network's "representations" of different functions; when a meta-learned network rapidly learns to implement a specific function, all of its adapted parameter values can be concatenated into a single vector that we treat as representing the function. We find that such parameter vectors can be added and subtracted according to symbolic relationships among the functions they represent, yielding new parameter vectors that successfully represent the functions predicted by the corresponding symbolic manipulations: the networks specified by these artificially recombined vectors actually implement the intended functions without any direct training on them. Our results suggest that meta-learning can tune a network's starting point to organize subsequent learning along systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through the space of possible parameter vectors, providing a geometric basis for realizing inductive biases in neural networks.

item.title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Nils Leutenegger
arXiv:2611.15533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell. Raw correlation-distance representational similarity analysis (RSA) covaried with the alignment of model and voxel patterns with the unit-mean profile (Spearman 0.97 across our networks, 0.79 across six ImageNet architectures); the advantage was absent from the component orthogonal to the mean profile, and the parallel component alone did not resolve it. On the unweighted angular component of centred patterns, trained networks were ahead at V1 (our network and 5 of 6 ImageNet models) and at LOC (all seven); the norm-weighted angular term was not resolved. A luminance-and-contrast bank scored above every network under ridge (point estimates), and adding network features under a shared penalty did not improve prediction. Intervals are stimulus-bootstrap intervals for three subjects, and 6 pre-stated predictions were not met. We recommend reporting sensitivity to centring over the evaluated stimuli on both sides, reporting components separately, and including a small multiverse and simple baselines.

item.title: Interpreting Brain Responses to Language with Sparse Features from Language Models
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Michael A. Lepori, Kendrick Kay, Greta Tuckute
arXiv:2606.06857v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A central goal of cognitive neuroscience is to characterize the features that are represented by human language cortex. Artificial language models (LMs) have emerged as a powerful tool to address this challenge, but studies relating biological and artificial representations are often criticized as relating one black box to another. The present work introduces Augmented Sparse Encoding Models, an encoding framework that replaces dense LM hidden states with hierarchically-organized sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, while explicitly including surprisal as a predictor. Using this approach, we (i) produce interpretations of neural responses and (ii) test whether model-brain alignment reflects primary or idiosyncratic variation in LM representations. Using a high-field 7T fMRI dataset of eight participants listening to 200 linguistically diverse sentences, we first validate our modeling framework by recovering previous interpretations of voxel populations tuned to processing difficulty and meaning abstractness. We then interpret a previously-uncharacterized (but reliable) voxel population and find that it is tuned to people-related content. Next, we show that the fronto-temporal human language network is predicted by a common set of features across its constituent regions, but find that frontal regions are relatively well-explained by surprisal alone, even in the absence of LM-based features. Finally, we show that brain responses are best explained by the features that tend to capture the most general information encoded in LM representations, suggesting a nontrivial correspondence between brain and LM language representation.

item.title: DUNE: Disentangling Polysemantic Neurons Without Losing Predictive Performance
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Do\u{g}ukan Ba\u{g}c{\i}, Bernt Schiele, Simone Schaub-Meyer, Jonas Fischer, Robin Hesse
arXiv:2605.31304v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely used, but understanding what they actually learn remains difficult. A major obstacle is that individual neurons often respond to multiple unrelated concepts, obscuring the network's internal decision process. Existing approaches, such as sparse autoencoders, can disentangle these mixed signals into more meaningful, ``monosemantic'' features, but typically introduce approximation errors that may degrade downstream performance. Consequently, these methods exhibit a Pareto frontier between monosemanticity and functional faithfulness. To address this, we introduce DUNE (disentangling units with no error), a method that decomposes DNN neurons into more monosemantic subunits while preserving their original function by design. DUNE identifies concept-specific contributions from the preceding layer and re-routes them into separate subunits whose aggregation exactly recovers the original activation. DUNE can be applied directly to pretrained models, without labels or training of an auxiliary model. Across several models, including DINOv2, DUNE achieves state-of-the-art or competitive monosemanticity while exactly preserving functional faithfulness, substantially advancing the existing Pareto frontier between these properties. DUNE operates efficiently and enables fine-grained interventions such as concept-specific steering.

item.title: Incremental Learning of Sparse Attention Patterns in Transformers
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
O\u{g}uz Kaan Y\"uksel, Rodrigo Alvarez Lucendo, Nicolas Flammarion
arXiv:2602.19143v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transformers integrate information from multiple past positions through sparse attention patterns that copy from specific locations. We study how these patterns form during training in a high-order Markov-chain setting, where the next token depends on several groups of past positions with differing statistical importance. Learning proceeds in discrete stages, each marked by the emergence of a sparse attention pattern for the next most important group. The dynamics are initially competitive, with all attention heads focusing on the dominant pattern, but later become cooperative, with different heads specializing in distinct patterns. For a tractable surrogate, the dynamics reduce to those of a tensor factorization problem, enabling us to prove stagewise convergence. Empirically, the number of stages completed depends on training set size, suggesting a form of implicit complexity control through early stopping. Overall, we give a theoretical account of how structured attention patterns and head specialization emerge without an explicit curriculum.

item.title: The thalamic reticular nucleus provides spatially and temporally tuned inhibition to the lateral geniculate nucleus across species
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Miao, Y., Ciftcioglu, U. M., Gorin, A. S., Dakwala, R., Ahn, S., Sommer, F. T., Hirsch, J. A.
By proposing a role in spatial attention, Francis Crick piqued interest in the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), a GABAergic structure that receives input from relay cells projecting to cortex and feeds back inhibition in return. Importantly, predictions of Crick's hypothesis extend beyond attention to suggest that TRN provides selective, localized inhibition to relay cells and, thus, influences sensory processing per se. To ask if this latter role for TRN holds across species, we compared previous recordings from cat with a novel dataset from mouse, focusing on vision. We estimated receptive field size and structure of reticular cells in the visual sector of TRN and of relay cells in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN). Cells in both nuclei encoded specific visual features and had receptive fields of comparable size within binocular visual space. Moreover, paired recordings from both structures suggested that TRN is able to promote burst firing in dLGN in addition to modulating spike rate. Thus, TRN is not only important for attentional regulation, but is also able to make fine-tuned contributions to early sensory processing.

item.title: There Will Be a Scientific Theory of Deep Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Jamie Simon, Daniel Kunin, Alexander Atanasov, Enric Boix-Adser\`a, Blake Bordelon, Jeremy Cohen, Nikhil Ghosh, Florentin Guth, Arthur Jacot, Mason Kamb, Dhruva Karkada, Eric J. Michaud, Berkan Ottlik, Joseph Turnbull
arXiv:2604.21691v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we make the case that a scientific theory of deep learning is emerging. By this we mean a theory which characterizes important properties and statistics of the training process, hidden representations, final weights, and performance of neural networks. We pull together major strands of ongoing research in deep learning theory and identify five growing bodies of work that point toward such a theory: (a) solvable idealized settings that provide intuition for learning dynamics in realistic systems; (b) tractable limits that reveal insights into fundamental learning phenomena; (c) simple mathematical laws that capture important macroscopic observables; (d) theories of hyperparameters that disentangle them from the rest of the training process, leaving simpler systems behind; and (e) universal behaviors shared across systems and settings which clarify which phenomena call for explanation. Taken together, these bodies of work share certain broad traits: they are concerned with the dynamics of the training process; they primarily seek to describe coarse aggregate statistics; and they emphasize falsifiable quantitative predictions. We argue that the emerging theory is best thought of as a mechanics of the learning process, and suggest the name learning mechanics. We discuss the relationship between this mechanics perspective and other approaches for building a theory of deep learning, including the statistical and information-theoretic perspectives. In particular, we anticipate a symbiotic relationship between learning mechanics and mechanistic interpretability. We also review and address common arguments that fundamental theory will not be possible or is not important. We conclude with a portrait of important open directions in learning mechanics and advice for beginners. We host further introductory materials, perspectives, and open questions at learningmechanics.pub.

item.title: A neural circuit for stereopsis in the fly
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Mearns, D. S., Park, Y., Shin, I., Murthy, M.
Stereopsis involves combining different views from the two eyes to infer depth, an ability that has intrigued neuroscientists for almost two centuries (Wheatstone, 1838). It enables insects such as the praying mantis to estimate the distance of prey (Nityananda et al., 2018), or primates to fixate objects at different depths (Cumming and Judge, 1986; Rashbass and Westheimer, 1961). While theoretical models for stereopsis have been proposed based on neural activity recordings (Marr and Poggio, 1976; Grossberg, 1983; Ohzawa et al., 1990), we do not have a detailed circuit mechanism for stereopsis founded on neural wiring. Here we achieve this in the fly, Drosophila melanogaster, by analyzing two whole-brain connectomes (Dorkenwald et al., 2024; Berg et al., 2026). Flies have sufficient overlap between the eyes to utilize binocular vision (Kemppainen et al., 2022); however, a circuit that performs stereopsis has not been uncovered in this model system. We show that a cell type that connects the two optic lobes called LC14 (Otsuna and Ito, 2006) forms a recurrent circuit across the brain that is capable of depth estimation. By building a connectome-constrained model, we demonstrate that recurrence is critical for binocular distance tuning in this circuit. Tuning is optimal for the size and distances of social targets (other flies), and we uncover a pathway within the brain specific for binocular vision computations. Silencing LC14 neurons renders this downstream circuitry sensitive to only monocular information and alters distance-dependent courtship behaviors, while activation of LC14 neurons causes flies to slow in response to an illusory object in their binocular visual field. In sum, we predict function from structure, uncovering how the fly brain computes distance from binocular cues, and identify a role for binocular vision in patterning social behavior.

item.title: SPIRE: Task-agnostic embodied continual learning through autonomous situation inference and causal motor-primitive reuse
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Yiyang Jia, Mingyang Lyu, Gongce Cao, Feifei Zhao, Yinqian Sun, Yi Zeng
arXiv:2611.14840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied continual learning requires controllers to infer changing situations, retain prior behavior and reuse motor skills without task labels or known boundaries. The challenge is deciding when to recover earlier behavior and which skills can support new learning. We introduce Situation-guided Primitive Integration for Recurrent Embodiment (SPIRE), a recurrent-spiking system that infers latent contexts from action-outcome evidence and learns context-specific motor actors online. Mature actors become protected sources that combine with a target-context residual to drive recurrent-spiking motor populations. Across coordinate, three-joint and hidden-force control, SPIRE maintained control, autonomously inferred situations, retained prior behavior and accelerated acquisition of an unseen source composition, reducing mean interactions to criterion by approximately 40% relative to matched fresh controllers. Rewinding compatible source actors impaired early acquisition in every matched intervention, demonstrating causal reuse. Against seven recurrent continual-learning and modular-control comparators, SPIRE achieved 2.4 times the mean prior-learning advantage of the strongest eligible task-free alternative selected for each paired stream. These results demonstrate autonomous recovery and causal reuse of motor skills for new learning in continuous embodied control.

item.title: Recognizing Mind Wandering: A Computational Phenomenology of Focused-Attention Meditation
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Prakash Chandra Kavi, Daniel Ari Friedman, Gustavo Patow
arXiv:2607.14833v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mind wandering often continues without recognition, raising a question about the relationship between attention and consciousness. How can a distraction be experienced before it is recognized as an attentional lapse, and what does recognition change? We address it for mind wandering, a form of spontaneous thought, during focused-attention meditation on the breath, through a computational phenomenology informed by Buddhist analyses of mind and meditation neuroscience. In an active-inference-inspired three-layer architecture, mental contents, termed thoughtseeds, are inferred from simulated large-scale brain network activity and compete for a capacity-limited global workspace, whose selection parallels Bengio's consciousness prior, while a separate graded monitor supports discrete recognition of lapses. Within a specified cycle of Breath Focus, Mind Wandering, Meta Awareness and Redirect Attention, recognition could begin while a distraction still held the workspace, an overlap that was usually brief. Stochastic monitoring checks also allowed intermittent recognition during ongoing wandering, with long intervals unrecognized. Recognition releases stabilization of the current regime and modulates the return policy in Meta Awareness, while return remains possible without it. Breath re-entry, recognition and redirection need not coincide. The model thus separates access to distracting content, monitoring of attention and recognition of a lapse, and shows how awareness of wandering can change its regulation without immediately ending it. This framework could be adapted to other meditation practices, to practice-related differences between novice and expert meditators, and to modeling subjective experience in other cognitive tasks.

item.title: A spatially continuous cell-type atlas reveals multiscale organization of the human cortex
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Lei, W., Tian, X., Dong, C., Lou, J., Zhao, X., Dong, X., Du, L., Yang, R., Hong, Y., Yu, Y., Yang, C., Qian, L., Liu, S., Li, A., Wang, M., Liu, B.
Neuroimaging has increasingly revealed fine-grained spatial heterogeneity within the human cortex, uncovering regional differentiation beyond conventional cortical divisions. However, understanding the cellular architecture underlying these imaging features requires spatially continuous cell-type references that capture both cortex-wide organization and regional specialization. Here, we introduce RIDGE (Regional Integration of Deconvolution with Guided Estimation), a deconvolution framework that anchors multiple regional references to continuous cortex-wide transcriptomic maps, thereby recovering cortex-wide organizational patterns while supporting region-specific cell-type inference. RIDGE reconstructs spatially continuous distributions of 24 major cortical cell types across the human cortex. The resulting maps are robust across analytical pipelines and independent reference datasets, recover established cell-type associations with known cortical features, and recapitulate the canonical primary sensory-allocortical/periallocortical (Pr-Al) axis of cortical cellular organization. At finer scales, RIDGE resolves distinct cellular profiles across default mode, motor, and visual systems, revealing local cellular specialization within each system. By relating these cellular maps to cortical imaging features, we demonstrate their utility for investigating cellular contributions to global cortical organization and regional specialization. Together, RIDGE provides a unified framework and spatially continuous cellular reference resource for integrating cellular architecture with human cortical imaging across spatial scales.

item.title: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
\"Omer Tekin Yavuz (\.Ileti\c{s}im Yaz{\i}l{\i}m)
arXiv:2611.13885v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interpretability demonstrations often show that intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer. A recent example removes an 18-neuron group in Qwen3-32B and the model answers "Simba" instead of "Scar" to a two-hop Lion King riddle. Such a demonstration establishes that the group matters, but not how much of it is necessary, whether other groups could do the same, or whether the effect carries over to other inputs. We ask: when intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer, how much of that group is actually necessary? For every selected group we measure all 4,096 subsets of 12 MLP neurons. On a two-alternative capital task (Qwen3-0.6B), zero-ablating 12 selected neurons lowers the answer margin by 27% while random neurons barely change it, yet replacing the same neurons with their values from other questions also barely changes it: their activations are nearly constant across questions, and we find no evidence that they carry question-specific content. On two-hop relation chains, patching 12 neurons with activations from the first-hop question shifts the answer to the bridge entity (from Scar to Simba): the greedy answer starts with the bridge in 9/11 chains for Qwen3-1.7B, 9/11 for Llama-3.2-1B and 8/10 for Gemma-3-1B; random neurons never do. The full group is rarely necessary: a few neurons often suffice, and in many chains disjoint subsets each flip the answer on their own, in an exploratory analysis most often when the model is less confident. Group effects transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other tested chains. We study neuron-level causal interventions and alternative subsets; we do not recover the full connectivity of circuits.

item.title: EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Python Song, Zhixuan Liang, Kelsey Fu, Mengdi Wang, Junfeng Yang, Shilong Liu
arXiv:2610.10498v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that autonomously decides where to explore next and turns the resulting physical interaction into improved code and skills. EmbodiedRSI realizes this through a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, in which competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish these hypotheses. Their outcomes guide Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, and Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory according to their value for later Fast-System improvement. On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI reaches 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. EmbodiedRSI also reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. Beyond benchmark performance, EmbodiedRSI transfers zero-shot to real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.

item.title: Goal Encoding in LLMs
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Arnab Sen Sharma, Eric Todd, Sheridan Feucht, Andy Arditi, Rohit Gandikota, Natalie Shapira, Gabriele Sarti, Constanza Fierro, Lisa Schut, David Bau
arXiv:2611.17297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.
